title: Hospitality
tomorrow: at the same dinner, guests grab the best seats. what does Jesus say?

lines: CALL THE POOR, THE LAME, THE BLIND.
cards: Dinner invitations can run on a quiet ledger: they had us over, so we owe them one.

Luke says Jesus, at a dinner himself, told his host to tear up the ledger: “when thou makest a feast, call the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind: And thou shalt be blessed; for they cannot recompense thee.”
Invite the ones who can't pay you back. That's the point, not the problem.

teach.b: So, one question: why open the table at all? Paul tells the Romans to be “given to hospitality,” and First Peter adds “without grudging.” Behind them stands an old scene.
Abraham sits at his tent door in the heat of the day, sees three strangers, and runs to meet them. He bows, has cakes baked, a calf prepared, and stands by them under the tree while they eat.
Now a neighbor who tells it too. Muslims know this scene from the Qur'an, as the story of Abraham's honored guests.
And the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, is reported in the hadith collection of al-Bukhari to have said that whoever believes in God and the Last Day should honor his guest.
Shared: a guest at the door is a matter of faith, not just manners. One honest difference. In Genesis, the visitors eat.
In the Qur'an they are messengers who don't touch the food, and Abraham is uneasy until they bring their news. Christians add their own reading: some see a hint of the Trinity in the three visitors.
Different windows on the same tent.
What both tellings share is the running. Abraham doesn't wait to be asked.

how: Christians practice hospitality through shared meals, church suppers and welcoming newcomers; some communities keep houses of hospitality open to anyone in need, and some icons show Abraham's three visitors at table.

o: making room at your table for a guest
repaying a dinner invitation in kind
decorating your home for visitors to admire

games.q: the open table — tap the pairs.

s: hospitality in the Bible means hosting the people who'll host you back
Jesus says call the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind: they cannot recompense thee.
the Qur'an also tells of Abraham's guests
Muslims know it as the story of Abraham's honored guests.
in both Genesis and the Qur'an, the visitors eat Abraham's meal
in Genesis they eat; in the Qur'an, the messengers don't touch it.

games.q: a Muslim family moves in next door and has you over for dinner; their dad keeps refilling your plate. you want to return the welcome. what fits both traditions' honoring of guests?
o: invite them over, ask what they eat, and serve them generously.
keep it simple; hospitality is mostly a matter of polite manners.
wait until you've studied their religion, so you can't offend.
games.why: both traditions treat the guest as a matter of faith. ask about food, then do what Abraham did: hurry, and set the table.

practice: Count on your fingers the people who have fed you at their table: family, friends, a neighbor, a church supper, a stranger. Let each face come back for a breath.
Then choose one person you could invite to yours, someone who isn't likely to invite you back.

wordCard.voice: Hospitality. Making room at your table and in your time for a guest, especially one who can't repay.

orig.note: Greek: love of strangers. 'hospitality' in Romans 12:13.

carryVoice: For the road: the open table, set for someone who can't pay you back. Until tomorrow.
